# Silmulator

**SIL/HIL/CIL Hardware Simulator** — A PyQt6 GUI application for debugging embedded software against simulated lab instruments that behave per their real device specifications.

## Documentation

| Guide | Description |
|---|---|
| [User Guide](docs/user_guide.md) | Installation, quick start, virtual hardware reference, troubleshooting |
| [Developer Guide](docs/developer_guide.md) | Architecture, device layer, GUI layer, adding devices |
| [Adding Blocks](docs/adding_blocks.md) | Step-by-step guide to creating new hardware blocks |
| [Architecture Diagrams](docs/architecture.md) | Mermaid diagrams: system overview, data flow, class hierarchy |
| [Docker Guide](docker/README.md) | Browser (NoVNC) and native window Docker usage |
| [C++ Core](cpp_core/README.md) | SCPI parser build, API reference, Doxygen instructions |
| [Python Package](silmulator/README.md) | Package structure, library API reference |
| [Word User Guide](docs/Silmulator_User_Guide.docx) | Official Microsoft Word version for distribution |

## Overview

Silmulator provides a drag-and-drop canvas where you place virtual hardware blocks — oscilloscopes, power supplies, function generators, multimeters, and MSP430 microcontrollers — connect them with virtual wires, and interact with them using real SCPI commands. A code-input block parses your C/C++/Python source and routes the SCPI calls to the connected devices.

This lets you test and debug measurement code **without physical hardware**, catching command errors and response-handling bugs at your desk.

## Architecture

```
Silmulator/
├── main.py                        # CLI entry point
├── setup.py                       # pip install support
├── requirements.txt               # Python dependencies
├── CMakeLists.txt                 # C++ build root
│
├── cpp_core/                      # High-performance C++ SCPI parser
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   ├── include/
│   │   ├── scpi_parser.h          # Parser class declaration
│   │   └── scpi_types.h           # ScpiCommand, ScpiToken, etc.
│   └── src/
│       ├── scpi_parser.cpp        # Parser implementation
│       └── bindings.cpp           # pybind11 Python bindings
│
└── silmulator/                    # Python package
    ├── app.py                     # Application entry point
    ├── scpi/
    │   └── parser.py              # Pure-Python SCPI parser (fallback)
    ├── devices/
    │   ├── base_device.py         # Abstract SCPI device base
    │   ├── oscilloscope.py        # Tektronix MSO54-compatible
    │   ├── power_supply.py        # Keysight E36312A-compatible
    │   ├── function_generator.py  # Keysight 33522B-compatible
    │   ├── multimeter.py          # Keysight 34401A-compatible
    │   └── msp430.py              # TI MSP430FR5994-compatible
    ├── gui/
    │   ├── main_window.py         # PyQt6 main window
    │   ├── canvas.py              # Drag-and-drop scene + view
    │   └── blocks/
    │       ├── base_block.py      # Abstract block base class
    │       ├── oscilloscope_block.py
    │       ├── power_supply_block.py
    │       ├── function_generator_block.py
    │       ├── multimeter_block.py
    │       ├── msp430_block.py
    │       └── code_input_block.py
    ├── code_parser/
    │   └── base_parser.py         # C/C++/Python SCPI extractor
    └── utils/
        ├── waveform.py            # Waveform generation (numpy)
        └── signals.py             # Qt signal bus
```

## Simulated Instruments

### Oscilloscope (Tektronix MSO54-compatible)
- 4 analog channels (CH1–CH4)
- Full `ACQ`, `CH`, `CURSOR`, `DATA`, `DISPLAY`, `HORIZONTAL`, `MEASUREMENT`, `SELECT`, `TRIGGER`, `WFMPRE` command trees
- Waveform generation and `CURVE?` data transfer (ASCII and binary encoding)
- Live waveform injection via `inject_waveform(source, array)`
- 8 configurable measurements: FREQUENCY, PERIOD, AMPLITUDE, RMS, MEAN, HIGH, LOW, PK2PK, RISE, FALL, PDUTY, NDUTY

### Power Supply (Keysight E36312A-compatible)
- 3 independent channels
- `SOURCE:VOLTAGE`, `SOURCE:CURRENT`, `OUTPUT`, `MEASURE`, `TRIGGER`, `INSTRUMENT` command trees
- OVP/OCP protection simulation
- `APPLY` combined set command
- Channel-by-channel tracking mode

### Function Generator (Keysight 33522B-compatible)
- 2 independent channels (SOURCE1, SOURCE2)
- Functions: SIN, SQU, RAMP, PULS, NOIS, DC, USER, ARB
- AM, FM, PM, PWM modulation
- Burst and sweep modes
- Arbitrary waveform catalog

### Multimeter (Keysight 34401A-compatible)
- Functions: VOLT:DC, VOLT:AC, CURR:DC, CURR:AC, RES, FRES, FREQ, PER, CONT, DIOD, TEMP
- `CONFIGURE`, `MEASURE`, `READ`, `FETCH`, `INITIATE` modes
- `CALCULATE` (null, limits, dB, statistics)
- `TRIGGER` and `SAMPLE` subsystems
- `DATA` buffer with `INITIATE`/`FETCH` workflow
- Measurement injection via `inject(function, value)`

### MSP430 (TI MSP430FR5994-compatible)
- 8 GPIO ports (P1–P8) with direction, pull-up/down, interrupt control
- 12-channel 12-bit ADC with voltage injection
- 3x Timer_A, 1x Timer_B with capture-compare
- 4x UART (eUSCI_A) with full serial config
- 2x SPI (eUSCI_B) with CPOL/CPHA and transfer simulation
- 4x I2C with address, frequency, master/slave modes
- Unified Clock System (DCO, LFXT, SMCLK, MCLK, ACLK)
- Power management modes (AM, LPM0–LPM4.5)
- 16-register CPU state, PC control, memory map read/write

## SCPI Command Examples

```python
from silmulator.devices import Oscilloscope, PowerSupply, FunctionGenerator

# Oscilloscope
osc = Oscilloscope()
osc.process("CH1:SCALE 0.5")           # 500mV/div
osc.process("HOR:SCALE 1E-3")          # 1ms/div
osc.process("TRIG:A:EDGE:SOURCE CH1")
osc.process("TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5")
osc.process("ACQ:STATE 1")             # Run
freq = osc.process("MEASUREMENT:MEAS1:TYPE FREQUENCY; VALUE?")
data = osc.process("CURVE?")           # Get waveform data

# Power Supply
psu = PowerSupply()
psu.process("INST:NSEL 1")
psu.process("VOLT 3.3")
psu.process("CURR 1.0")
psu.process("OUTP ON")
voltage = psu.process("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")

# Function Generator
fgen = FunctionGenerator()
fgen.process("SOURCE1:FUNC SIN")
fgen.process("SOURCE1:FREQ 1000")
fgen.process("SOURCE1:VOLT 2.0")
fgen.process("OUTPUT1 ON")

# MSP430
mcu = MSP430()
mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:DIRECTION 0xFF")  # All outputs
mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0x01")     # P1.0 HIGH
mcu.process("ADC:CHANNEL0:INJECT 1.65")  # Inject 1.65V
raw = mcu.process("ADC:CONVERT 0")       # Read raw ADC value
```

## C++ Core

The C++ SCPI parser (`cpp_core/`) provides a high-performance parsing backend with pybind11 Python bindings. It is optional — the pure-Python `silmulator/scpi/parser.py` is used automatically when the C++ extension is not built.

### Building the C++ extension

```bash
mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..
make -j4
# Copy the resulting scpi_core.so to silmulator/scpi/
```

## Code Parser

The `CodeInputBlock` on the canvas parses C, C++, or Python source code to extract SCPI command strings:

**Recognized C/C++ patterns:**
```c
viWrite(session, "VOLT 5.0");
viQueryf(session, "MEAS:VOLT:DC?", result);
visa_write(dev, "OUTP ON");
scpi_send(handle, "ACQ:STATE 1");
ibwrt(dev, "TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5");
```

**Recognized Python patterns:**
```python
inst.write("VOLT 5.0")
result = inst.query("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")
rm.open_resource("GPIB::1").write("OUTP ON")
```

## GUI Usage

1. **Launch:** `python main.py`
2. **Add blocks:** Double-click items in the Library panel, or click toolbar buttons
3. **Connect blocks:** Click a port circle on one block, drag to a port on another
4. **Send commands:** Select a block → right-click → "Send SCPI command", or use the SCPI Console at the bottom
5. **Paste code:** Add a "Code Input" block → double-click to open the editor → paste your C/C++/Python code → click "Parse" to extract SCPI commands
6. **Run commands:** After connecting a Code Input block to hardware blocks, right-click → "Run parsed commands"
7. **Save/Load layouts:** File → Save (`.sil` JSON format)

### Keyboard shortcuts

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `Delete` | Remove selected blocks |
| `Ctrl+A` | Select all |
| `Ctrl+N` | New canvas |
| `Ctrl+O` | Open layout |
| `Ctrl+S` | Save layout |
| `Ctrl+0` | Reset zoom |
| `Ctrl+Shift+F` | Fit all blocks in view |
| Middle mouse drag | Pan |
| Scroll wheel | Zoom in/out |

## Running Tests

```bash
# Install dependencies

# Run all tests
python -m pytest tests/ -v

# Run specific device tests
python -m pytest tests/test_oscilloscope.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_power_supply.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_function_generator.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_multimeter.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_msp430.py -v

```

- Python 3.9+
- PyQt6 >= 6.4.0
- numpy >= 1.24.0
- scipy >= 1.10.0

Optional (for C++ parser):
- CMake >= 3.16
- pybind11 >= 2.10.0
- C++17 compiler (GCC, Clang, or MSVC)

## Design Decisions

**SCPI compliance:** Each device implements the command set from its respective programmer's reference manual. Short forms (e.g., `VOLT` for `VOLTAGE`, `MEAS` for `MEASURE`) are registered alongside long forms for compatibility with real test code.

**Simulation fidelity:** Measurements return the configured/injected values plus a small Gaussian noise term (≈1e-5 relative), mimicking real instrument behavior. You can override this with `inject(function, value)` for deterministic testing.

**Pure-Python fallback:** The SCPI parser has both a C++ and Python implementation. The Python version is always available; the C++ version improves throughput for high-rate command streaming.

**State isolation:** Each device instance maintains fully independent state. Running `*RST` returns all parameters to their power-on defaults without affecting other devices.

# Silmulator

**SIL/HIL/CIL Hardware Simulator** — A PyQt6 GUI application for debugging embedded software against simulated lab instruments that behave per their real device specifications.

## Documentation

| Guide | Description |
|---|---|
| [User Guide](docs/user_guide.md) | Installation, quick start, virtual hardware reference, troubleshooting |
| [Developer Guide](docs/developer_guide.md) | Architecture, device layer, GUI layer, adding devices |
| [Adding Blocks](docs/adding_blocks.md) | Step-by-step guide to creating new hardware blocks |
| [Architecture Diagrams](docs/architecture.md) | Mermaid diagrams: system overview, data flow, class hierarchy |
| [Docker Guide](docker/README.md) | Browser (NoVNC) and native window Docker usage |
| [C++ Core](cpp_core/README.md) | SCPI parser build, API reference, Doxygen instructions |
| [Python Package](silmulator/README.md) | Package structure, library API reference |
| [Word User Guide](docs/Silmulator_User_Guide.docx) | Official Microsoft Word version for distribution |

## Overview

Silmulator provides a drag-and-drop canvas where you place virtual hardware blocks — oscilloscopes, power supplies, function generators, multimeters, and MSP430 microcontrollers — connect them with virtual wires, and interact with them using real SCPI commands. A code-input block parses your C/C++/Python source and routes the SCPI calls to the connected devices.

This lets you test and debug measurement code **without physical hardware**, catching command errors and response-handling bugs at your desk.

## Architecture

```
Silmulator/
├── main.py                        # CLI entry point
├── setup.py                       # pip install support
├── requirements.txt               # Python dependencies
├── CMakeLists.txt                 # C++ build root
│
├── cpp_core/                      # High-performance C++ SCPI parser
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   ├── include/
│   │   ├── scpi_parser.h          # Parser class declaration
│   │   └── scpi_types.h           # ScpiCommand, ScpiToken, etc.
│   └── src/
│       ├── scpi_parser.cpp        # Parser implementation
│       └── bindings.cpp           # pybind11 Python bindings
│
└── silmulator/                    # Python package
    ├── app.py                     # Application entry point
    ├── scpi/
    │   └── parser.py              # Pure-Python SCPI parser (fallback)
    ├── devices/
    │   ├── base_device.py         # Abstract SCPI device base
    │   ├── oscilloscope.py        # Tektronix MSO54-compatible
    │   ├── power_supply.py        # Keysight E36312A-compatible
    │   ├── function_generator.py  # Keysight 33522B-compatible
    │   ├── multimeter.py          # Keysight 34401A-compatible
    │   └── msp430.py              # TI MSP430FR5994-compatible
    ├── gui/
    │   ├── main_window.py         # PyQt6 main window
    │   ├── canvas.py              # Drag-and-drop scene + view
    │   └── blocks/
    │       ├── base_block.py      # Abstract block base class
    │       ├── oscilloscope_block.py
    │       ├── power_supply_block.py
    │       ├── function_generator_block.py
    │       ├── multimeter_block.py
    │       ├── msp430_block.py
    │       └── code_input_block.py
    ├── code_parser/
    │   └── base_parser.py         # C/C++/Python SCPI extractor
    └── utils/
        ├── waveform.py            # Waveform generation (numpy)
        └── signals.py             # Qt signal bus
```

## Simulated Instruments

### Oscilloscope (Tektronix MSO54-compatible)
- 4 analog channels (CH1–CH4)
- Full `ACQ`, `CH`, `CURSOR`, `DATA`, `DISPLAY`, `HORIZONTAL`, `MEASUREMENT`, `SELECT`, `TRIGGER`, `WFMPRE` command trees
- Waveform generation and `CURVE?` data transfer (ASCII and binary encoding)
- Live waveform injection via `inject_waveform(source, array)`
- 8 configurable measurements: FREQUENCY, PERIOD, AMPLITUDE, RMS, MEAN, HIGH, LOW, PK2PK, RISE, FALL, PDUTY, NDUTY

### Power Supply (Keysight E36312A-compatible)
- 3 independent channels
- `SOURCE:VOLTAGE`, `SOURCE:CURRENT`, `OUTPUT`, `MEASURE`, `TRIGGER`, `INSTRUMENT` command trees
- OVP/OCP protection simulation
- `APPLY` combined set command
- Channel-by-channel tracking mode

### Function Generator (Keysight 33522B-compatible)
- 2 independent channels (SOURCE1, SOURCE2)
- Functions: SIN, SQU, RAMP, PULS, NOIS, DC, USER, ARB
- AM, FM, PM, PWM modulation
- Burst and sweep modes
- Arbitrary waveform catalog

### Multimeter (Keysight 34401A-compatible)
- Functions: VOLT:DC, VOLT:AC, CURR:DC, CURR:AC, RES, FRES, FREQ, PER, CONT, DIOD, TEMP
- `CONFIGURE`, `MEASURE`, `READ`, `FETCH`, `INITIATE` modes
- `CALCULATE` (null, limits, dB, statistics)
- `TRIGGER` and `SAMPLE` subsystems
- `DATA` buffer with `INITIATE`/`FETCH` workflow
- Measurement injection via `inject(function, value)`

### MSP430 (TI MSP430FR5994-compatible)
- 8 GPIO ports (P1–P8) with direction, pull-up/down, interrupt control
- 12-channel 12-bit ADC with voltage injection
- 3x Timer_A, 1x Timer_B with capture-compare
- 4x UART (eUSCI_A) with full serial config
- 2x SPI (eUSCI_B) with CPOL/CPHA and transfer simulation
- 4x I2C with address, frequency, master/slave modes
- Unified Clock System (DCO, LFXT, SMCLK, MCLK, ACLK)
- Power management modes (AM, LPM0–LPM4.5)
- 16-register CPU state, PC control, memory map read/write

## SCPI Command Examples

```python
from silmulator.devices import Oscilloscope, PowerSupply, FunctionGenerator

# Oscilloscope
osc = Oscilloscope()
osc.process("CH1:SCALE 0.5")           # 500mV/div
osc.process("HOR:SCALE 1E-3")          # 1ms/div
osc.process("TRIG:A:EDGE:SOURCE CH1")
osc.process("TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5")
osc.process("ACQ:STATE 1")             # Run
freq = osc.process("MEASUREMENT:MEAS1:TYPE FREQUENCY; VALUE?")
data = osc.process("CURVE?")           # Get waveform data

# Power Supply
psu = PowerSupply()
psu.process("INST:NSEL 1")
psu.process("VOLT 3.3")
psu.process("CURR 1.0")
psu.process("OUTP ON")
voltage = psu.process("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")

# Function Generator
fgen = FunctionGenerator()
fgen.process("SOURCE1:FUNC SIN")
fgen.process("SOURCE1:FREQ 1000")
fgen.process("SOURCE1:VOLT 2.0")
fgen.process("OUTPUT1 ON")

# MSP430
mcu = MSP430()
mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:DIRECTION 0xFF")  # All outputs
mcu.process("GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0x01")     # P1.0 HIGH
mcu.process("ADC:CHANNEL0:INJECT 1.65")  # Inject 1.65V
raw = mcu.process("ADC:CONVERT 0")       # Read raw ADC value
```

## C++ Core

The C++ SCPI parser (`cpp_core/`) provides a high-performance parsing backend with pybind11 Python bindings. It is optional — the pure-Python `silmulator/scpi/parser.py` is used automatically when the C++ extension is not built.

### Building the C++ extension

```bash
mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..
make -j4
# Copy the resulting scpi_core.so to silmulator/scpi/
```

## Code Parser

The `CodeInputBlock` on the canvas parses C, C++, or Python source code to extract SCPI command strings:

**Recognized C/C++ patterns:**
```c
viWrite(session, "VOLT 5.0");
viQueryf(session, "MEAS:VOLT:DC?", result);
visa_write(dev, "OUTP ON");
scpi_send(handle, "ACQ:STATE 1");
ibwrt(dev, "TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5");
```

**Recognized Python patterns:**
```python
inst.write("VOLT 5.0")
result = inst.query("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")
rm.open_resource("GPIB::1").write("OUTP ON")
```

## GUI Usage

1. **Launch:** `python main.py`
2. **Add blocks:** Double-click items in the Library panel, or click toolbar buttons
3. **Connect blocks:** Click a port circle on one block, drag to a port on another
4. **Send commands:** Select a block → right-click → "Send SCPI command", or use the SCPI Console at the bottom
5. **Paste code:** Add a "Code Input" block → double-click to open the editor → paste your C/C++/Python code → click "Parse" to extract SCPI commands
6. **Run commands:** After connecting a Code Input block to hardware blocks, right-click → "Run parsed commands"
7. **Save/Load layouts:** File → Save (`.sil` JSON format)

### Keyboard shortcuts

| Key | Action |
|-----|--------|
| `Delete` | Remove selected blocks |
| `Ctrl+A` | Select all |
| `Ctrl+N` | New canvas |
| `Ctrl+O` | Open layout |
| `Ctrl+S` | Save layout |
| `Ctrl+0` | Reset zoom |
| `Ctrl+Shift+F` | Fit all blocks in view |
| Middle mouse drag | Pan |
| Scroll wheel | Zoom in/out |

## Running Tests

```bash

# Run all tests

# Run specific device tests

python -m pytest tests/test_function_generator.py -v
python -m pytest tests/test_multimeter.py -v

python -m pytest tests/test_scpi_parser.py -v
```

## Requirements

- PyQt6 >= 6.4.0
- numpy >= 1.24.0
- scipy >= 1.10.0

Optional (for C++ parser):

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Build the Silmulator Python package (wheel + sdist) using uv.
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
cd "$SCRIPT_DIR"

echo "=== Silmulator Python Build ==="
echo ""

# ── dependency check ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if ! command -v uv &>/dev/null; then
    echo "Error: 'uv' not found."
    echo "Install it with:"
    echo "  curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh"
    echo "  # or: brew install uv"
    exit 1
fi

echo "uv $(uv --version)"
echo ""

# ── clean previous artifacts ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
rm -rf dist/ *.egg-info/ build/

# ── build ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
echo "Building wheel and source distribution..."
uv build

echo ""
echo "Artifacts:"
ls -lh dist/
echo ""
echo "Install locally with:"
echo "  uv pip install dist/silmulator-*.whl"
echo "  # or: pip install dist/silmulator-*.whl"
echo ""
echo "Run after install:"
echo "  silmulator"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Build a standalone, distributable installer for Silmulator.
#
#   macOS  → dist/Silmulator-1.0.0-macos-arm64.dmg   (drag-to-Applications)
#   Linux  → dist/Silmulator-1.0.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage  (run directly)
#
# Windows: use build_installer.bat instead.
#
# Prerequisites (all platforms):
#   Python 3.9+ with pip  |  uv (preferred)
#
# macOS extras (optional, for nicer DMG):
#   brew install create-dmg
#
# Linux extras (downloaded automatically if missing):
#   appimagetool (fetched from GitHub releases)
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
cd "$SCRIPT_DIR"

APP_NAME="Silmulator"
APP_VERSION="1.0.0"
DIST_DIR="$SCRIPT_DIR/dist"

echo "=== $APP_NAME $APP_VERSION — Installer Build ==="
echo ""

# ── detect platform ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
OS="$(uname -s)"
ARCH="$(uname -m)"
echo "Platform: $OS $ARCH"
echo ""

# ── pick Python / uv ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
if command -v uv &>/dev/null; then
    PY="uv run python"
    PIP="uv pip"
    echo "Using uv"
elif command -v python3 &>/dev/null; then
    PY="python3"
    PIP="python3 -m pip"
    echo "Using python3"
else
    echo "Error: Python 3 not found."
    exit 1
fi

# ── install PyInstaller if needed ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if ! $PY -c "import PyInstaller" 2>/dev/null; then
    echo "Installing PyInstaller..."
    $PIP install "pyinstaller>=6.0.0"
fi
echo "PyInstaller: $($PY -m PyInstaller --version)"
echo ""

# ── run PyInstaller ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
echo "Running PyInstaller..."
rm -rf build/ "$DIST_DIR/$APP_NAME" "$DIST_DIR/${APP_NAME}.app"
$PY -m PyInstaller silmulator.spec --noconfirm

echo ""
echo "PyInstaller complete."

# ── platform-specific packaging ───────────────────────────────────────────────
case "$OS" in

  # ── macOS → .dmg ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Darwin*)
    APP_BUNDLE="$DIST_DIR/${APP_NAME}.app"
    DMG_NAME="${APP_NAME}-${APP_VERSION}-macos-${ARCH}.dmg"
    DMG_OUT="$DIST_DIR/$DMG_NAME"

    echo "Creating macOS DMG: $DMG_NAME"

    if command -v create-dmg &>/dev/null; then
      # nice DMG with background & Applications symlink
      create-dmg \
        --volname "$APP_NAME" \
        --volicon "$APP_BUNDLE/Contents/Resources/app.icns" 2>/dev/null || true \

@echo off
:: Build a standalone Windows installer for Silmulator.
::
:: Output:
::   dist\Silmulator-1.0.0-windows-installer.exe   (if NSIS is installed)
::   dist\Silmulator-1.0.0-windows.zip              (always, as fallback)
::
:: Prerequisites:
::   Python 3.9+  (python.exe must be on PATH)
::   pip          (bundled with Python)
::
:: Optional (for a proper .exe installer):
::   NSIS 3.x     https://nsis.sourceforge.io/Download
::                After install, ensure "makensis" is on PATH or in the default
::                install location C:\Program Files (x86)\NSIS\makensis.exe

setlocal enabledelayedexpansion

set APP_NAME=Silmulator
set APP_VERSION=1.0.0
set SCRIPT_DIR=%~dp0
set DIST_DIR=%SCRIPT_DIR%dist

echo === %APP_NAME% %APP_VERSION% -- Windows Installer Build ===
echo.

:: ── check Python ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
where python >nul 2>&1
if errorlevel 1 (
    echo Error: python.exe not found on PATH.
    echo Install Python 3.9+ from https://www.python.org/downloads/
    exit /b 1
)

for /f "tokens=*" %%v in ('python --version') do set PY_VER=%%v
echo Python: %PY_VER%

:: ── install PyInstaller ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
python -c "import PyInstaller" 2>nul
if errorlevel 1 (
    echo Installing PyInstaller...
    python -m pip install "pyinstaller>=6.0.0" --quiet
)
for /f "tokens=*" %%v in ('python -m PyInstaller --version') do set PI_VER=%%v
echo PyInstaller: %PI_VER%
echo.

:: ── install app dependencies ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
echo Installing app dependencies...
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt --quiet
echo.

:: ── run PyInstaller ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
echo Running PyInstaller...
if exist "%DIST_DIR%\%APP_NAME%" rmdir /s /q "%DIST_DIR%\%APP_NAME%"
if exist build rmdir /s /q build

python -m PyInstaller silmulator.spec --noconfirm
if errorlevel 1 (
    echo PyInstaller failed.
---
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=68", "wheel"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "silmulator"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "SIL/HIL/CIL hardware simulator with SCPI command support"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.9"
license = { text = "MIT" }
keywords = ["scpi", "sil", "hil", "cil", "simulator", "hardware", "instruments"]
classifiers = [
    "Development Status :: 4 - Beta",
    "Intended Audience :: Developers",
    "Topic :: Scientific/Engineering :: Interface Engine/Protocol Translator",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.9",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.10",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.11",
    "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.12",
]
dependencies = [
    "PyQt6>=6.4.0",
    "numpy>=1.24.0",
    "scipy>=1.10.0",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
dev = [
    "pybind11>=2.10.0",
    "pytest>=7.2.0",
    "pytest-qt>=4.2.0",
    "pyinstaller>=6.0.0",
]

[project.scripts]
silmulator = "silmulator.app:main"

[project.gui-scripts]
silmulator-gui = "silmulator.app:main"

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["."]
include = ["silmulator*"]

[tool.uv]
dev-dependencies = [
    "pybind11>=2.10.0",
    "pytest>=7.2.0",
    "pytest-qt>=4.2.0",
    "pyinstaller>=6.0.0",
]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
python_files = ["test_*.py"]
python_classes = ["Test*"]
python_functions = ["test_*"]

content.content:
# Silmulator — Docker Usage Guide

Silmulator ships two Docker configurations:

| Mode | File | Use case |
|---|---|---|
| Production (browser) | `Dockerfile` + `docker-compose.yml` | Any OS, no display setup needed |
| Development (native) | `Dockerfile.dev` + `docker-compose.dev.yml` | Live code edits, native window |

---

## Production Mode — Browser Access (NoVNC)

The application streams to your web browser over WebSockets. No VNC client, no display server, and no OS-specific setup required.

### Start

```bash
# From the Silmulator/ root directory
docker compose up -d
```

### Open the application

Navigate to **http://localhost:6080/vnc.html** in any modern browser.

When prompted for a password, enter: `silmulator`

### Stop

```bash
docker compose down
```

### Persist data between restarts

The compose file mounts a named volume `silmulator-config` to store layouts (`.sil` files) and settings across container restarts. No action needed — it is automatic.

To clear saved data:

```bash
docker compose down -v   # removes the named volume too
```

### Custom VNC password

```bash
VNC_PASSWORD=mysecretpassword docker compose up -d
```

Or set it in a `.env` file alongside `docker-compose.yml`:

```
VNC_PASSWORD=mysecretpassword
```

### Custom port

If port 6080 is occupied:

```bash
APP_PORT=8080 docker compose up -d
# → open http://localhost:8080/vnc.html
```

### Health check

```bash
docker compose ps          # shows health: healthy / starting / unhealthy
docker compose logs -f     # stream logs in real time
```

---

## Development Mode — Native Window

Useful when you are actively editing source code. The source directory is bind-mounted, so changes take effect immediately on the next launch without rebuilding the image.

### Prerequisites

**macOS:** Install [XQuartz](https://www.xquartz.org/), then in XQuartz Preferences → Security, enable "Allow connections from network clients". Restart XQuartz.

**Linux:** No extra setup; X11 is already running.

**Windows (WSL2):** Install [VcXsrv](https://sourceforge.net/projects/vcxsrv/) or [Xming](http://www.straightrunning.com/XmingNotes/). Set `DISPLAY=host.docker.internal:0`.

### Start

```bash
# macOS: allow Docker to connect to XQuartz
xhost +localhost

# Start the development container
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up
```

The Silmulator window opens on your desktop directly.

### Live editing

The container mounts `./silmulator` as read-write. Edit any `.py` file in `silmulator/`, then re-run `python main.py` inside the container:

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml exec silmulator-dev python main.py
```

### Building the C++ extension inside the container

The development image includes CMake, g++, and pybind11:

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml exec silmulator-dev bash
# Inside the container:
mkdir -p /app/build && cd /app/build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
make -j$(nproc)
cp scpi_core*.so /app/silmulator/scpi/
```

---

## Building Images Manually

### Production image

```bash
docker build -t silmulator:latest .
docker run -d -p 6080:6080 -e VNC_PASSWORD=silmulator silmulator:latest
```

### Development image

```bash
docker build -f Dockerfile.dev -t silmulator:dev .
docker run -it --rm \
  -e DISPLAY=$DISPLAY \
  -v /tmp/.X11-unix:/tmp/.X11-unix \
  -v $(pwd)/silmulator:/app/silmulator \
  silmulator:dev python main.py
```

---

## Image Internals

### Production (`Dockerfile`) — multi-stage build

**Stage 1: C++ builder**
- Base: `python:3.11-slim`
- Installs: `cmake`, `g++`, `libpython3-dev`, `pybind11-dev`
- Builds `scpi_core.so`

**Stage 2: Runtime**
- Base: `python:3.11-slim`
- Copies the built `.so` from stage 1
- Installs: Qt6 X11 libraries, Xvfb, x11vnc, NoVNC, fluxbox
- Installs Python deps from `requirements.txt`
- Copies application source
- Exposes ports: `5900` (VNC), `6080` (NoVNC web)
- Entrypoint: `docker/entrypoint.sh`

### Development (`Dockerfile.dev`)
- Single stage based on `python:3.11`
- All build tools included
- Source is bind-mounted at runtime — not copied into the image
- No VNC stack; uses `DISPLAY` environment variable for X11 forwarding

---

## Ports Reference

| Port | Protocol | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 5900 | TCP | Raw VNC (for VNC client apps) |
| 6080 | HTTP/WS | NoVNC web browser access |

---

## Volume Reference

| Volume | Mount point | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `silmulator-config` | `/root/.config/silmulator` | Saved layouts, settings |

---

## Troubleshooting

**Browser shows "Connection failed"**
- Wait 10–15 seconds after `docker compose up -d`; the VNC server takes a moment to start.
- Run `docker compose logs` and look for `x11vnc is ready`.

**VNC password prompt loops**
- Default password: `silmulator`
- To reset the volume: `docker compose down -v && docker compose up -d`

**Blank or black screen in browser**
- The window manager (fluxbox) may still be initializing. Wait 5 seconds and refresh.

**X11 errors in development mode (macOS)**
- Make sure XQuartz is running and `xhost +localhost` was run in a terminal (not inside the container).
- Verify `DISPLAY` is set: `echo $DISPLAY` should return `:0` or `host.docker.internal:0`.

**"cannot connect to X server" in development mode (Linux)**
- Run `xhost +local:docker` on the host before starting the container.

Lesson 0003

Running Silmulator on Windows, Mac & Linux

Know all four launch paths so you can get the app running in any environment — dev machine, Docker, or end-user install.

Lesson progress

0 / 6 sections complete

01 The Four Ways to Run Silmulator

Every launch path ultimately runs the same Python entry point — silmulator/app.py:main() — called via main.py. What differs is how the dependencies are installed and how the display is set up.

ALL Dev mode

Clone + pip/uv install deps + python main.py. Fastest for development; no packaging step.

Docker Browser

docker compose up, then open localhost:6080. Runs on any OS with no display drivers.

macOS Installer

build_installer.sh → .dmg. Drag Silmulator.app to Applications; launch like any app.

Windows Installer

build_installer.bat → .exe (NSIS) or .zip. Run the installer; start from Start Menu.

Linux AppImage

build_installer.sh → .AppImage. Mark executable; double-click or run from terminal.

02 Dev Mode — Direct Python Launch All platforms

This is what you use every day as the developer. The project uses uv to manage the virtual environment, but plain pip works too.

  1. Install Python 3.9+ — Win use the Microsoft Store or winget install Python.Python.3.11. Mac brew install python@3.11 or the official .pkg. Linux sudo apt install python3.11 or dnf install python3.
  2. Install uv (recommended): 
    # macOS / Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
  3. Clone & enter the project: 
    git clone <repo-url> Silmulator
cd Silmulator/Silmulator
  4. Install dependencies: 
    # with uv (creates .venv automatically)
uv sync

# OR with pip
pip install -r requirements.txt
  5. Launch: 
    # with uv
uv run python main.py

# OR with activated venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # macOS / Linux
.venv\Scripts\activate       # Windows
python main.py

Where does this lead in code? main.py is a two-liner:

# Silmulator/main.py
import sys
from silmulator.app import main   # → silmulator/app.py:main()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())               # exits with the Qt event loop return code
💡
After pip install -e . (editable install), the command silmulator becomes available as a terminal command on any platform — it calls the same silmulator.app:main via pyproject.toml's [project.scripts] entry.

03 Docker — Browser Launch Any OS

Docker is the easiest cross-platform method: no Python install, no display drivers, no PyQt6 version headaches. The container runs Xvfb (virtual framebuffer) + VNC + NoVNC, and you connect via a browser.

  1. Install Docker Desktop for your platform. On Linux, Docker Engine is enough.
  2. Start the container: 
    cd Silmulator/   # repo root, where docker-compose.yml lives
docker compose up -d
  3. Open in browser: navigate to http://localhost:6080/vnc.html. Password: silmulator.
  4. Stop: docker compose down. Saved layouts persist in the silmulator-config named volume.

Useful variants:

# Change port if 6080 is taken
APP_PORT=8080 docker compose up -d

# Change the VNC password
VNC_PASSWORD=mysecret docker compose up -d

# Check health
docker compose ps        # shows "healthy" once VNC is ready
docker compose logs -f   # stream logs; look for "x11vnc is ready"
ℹ️
The production Dockerfile is a multi-stage build: stage 1 compiles the C++ SCPI extension (scpi_core.so) inside a builder image; stage 2 copies only the .so file into a slim runtime image with Qt6 and NoVNC. This keeps the final image small while bundling the optional C++ speedup automatically.

04 Standalone Installers — Ship to End Users

All three installer builds use PyInstaller (silmulator.spec) to bundle the Python interpreter, all dependencies, and the app into a single artifact that users can run without installing Python.

macOS → .dmg

  1. Ensure Python 3.9+ and optionally brew install create-dmg are available.
  2. Run: 
    ./build_installer.sh
  3. Output: dist/Silmulator-1.0.0-macos-arm64.dmg
  4. Distribute the DMG; users drag Silmulator.app to their Applications folder.
⚠️
macOS Gatekeeper will block unsigned apps on first launch. The user must right-click → Open to bypass this, or you need an Apple Developer certificate + codesign + notarytool for a smooth out-of-box experience.

Linux → .AppImage

  1. Run: 
    ./build_installer.sh
    (The script downloads appimagetool automatically if it's missing.)
  2. Output: dist/Silmulator-1.0.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage
  3. Distribute the AppImage; users mark it executable and run it: 
    chmod +x Silmulator-1.0.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage
./Silmulator-1.0.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage

Windows → .exe or .zip

  1. Open Command Prompt (not PowerShell — the script is a .bat).
  2. Optionally install NSIS 3.x for a proper installer .exe.
  3. Run: 
    build_installer.bat
  4. Output (with NSIS): dist\Silmulator-1.0.0-windows-installer.exe
    Output (without NSIS): dist\Silmulator-1.0.0-windows.zip — unzip and run Silmulator.exe inside.

05 Comparison — When to Use Which

Method Python needed? Needs display? Best for
python main.py ✓ Yes ✓ Native display Active development on any OS
uv run python main.py ✓ Yes (uv handles venv) ✓ Native display Dev — fastest first-time setup
silmulator (installed) ✓ Yes ✓ Native display Dev on a configured machine
Docker (browser / NoVNC) ✗ No ✗ No — browser only CI, remote machines, any OS with zero setup
Docker (dev / X11 forward) ✗ No ~ X11 server needed Dev inside container, live code edits
.dmg / .AppImage / .exe ✗ No — self-contained ✓ Native display Distributing to end users with no Python
💡
Often confused: Docker NoVNC mode vs X11 forwarding. NoVNC renders inside a full virtual X11 session inside the container and streams it to the browser — no local X server needed, works on any OS. X11 forwarding (dev mode) sends Qt draw calls to your local X server — faster and feels more native, but requires XQuartz (Mac), VcXsrv (Win), or a running X11 server (Linux).

Check Your Understanding

Q1. You want to run Silmulator on a remote Linux CI server with no display. Which launch method works?

  • python main.py directly on the server
  • docker compose up -d, then access via browser at :6080
  • Run the Linux AppImage on the server
  • uv run python main.py — uv handles the display setup

Q2. After running pip install -e ., which command launches Silmulator?

  • silmulator-gui (the gui-script entry is the only one)
  • silmulator
  • python main.py (the installed entry-point is only for packaged releases)
  • sil (short alias registered in setup.py)

Q3. On macOS, a user double-clicks Silmulator.app from the DMG and gets "Silmulator can't be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software." What is the quickest fix that does NOT require code-signing?

  • Disable Gatekeeper entirely: sudo spctl --master-disable
  • Run chmod +x Silmulator.app in Terminal first
  • Right-click (Control-click) → Open → confirm in the dialog
  • Drag to Applications first, then double-click from there

Q4. The Windows installer build produces a .zip instead of a .exe installer. Why?

  • PyInstaller on Windows always outputs a .zip; NSIS converts it to .exe later in a separate step.
  • Python is below 3.11, so NSIS cannot produce an .exe for that version.
  • NSIS (makensis) is not installed or not on PATH — the .bat falls back to zipping the PyInstaller output.
  • The machine is running Windows 10 or below; the .exe installer requires Windows 11.

Q5. You clone the repo on macOS and run uv sync — what does that do, specifically?

  • Compiles the C++ SCPI extension and installs all Python deps into the system Python.
  • Updates uv.lock to the latest package versions and installs them.
  • Creates (or updates) .venv with the exact package versions from uv.lock, without touching the system Python.
  • Syncs the local package cache with the PyPI remote index — downloads any packages that are out of date.

# Change the VNC password
VNC_PASSWORD=mysecret docker compose up -d

# Check health
docker compose ps        # shows "healthy" once VNC is ready
docker compose logs -f   # stream logs; look for "x11vnc is ready"
ℹ️
The production Dockerfile is a multi-stage build: stage 1 compiles the C++ SCPI extension (scpi_core.so) inside a builder image; stage 2 copies only the .so file into a slim runtime image with Qt6 and NoVNC. This keeps the final image small while bundling the optional C++ speedup automatically.

04 Standalone Installers — Ship to End Users

All three installer builds use PyInstaller (silmulator.spec) to bundle the Python interpreter, all dependencies, and the app into a single artifact that users can run without installing Python.

macOS → .dmg

  1. Ensure Python 3.9+ and optionally brew install create-dmg are available.
  2. Run: 
    ./build_installer.sh
  3. Output: dist/Silmulator-1.0.0-macos-arm64.dmg
  4. Distribute the DMG; users drag Silmulator.app to their Applications folder.
⚠️
macOS Gatekeeper will block unsigned apps on first launch. The user must right-click → Open to bypass this, or you need an Apple Developer certificate + codesign + notarytool for a smooth out-of-box experience.

Linux → .AppImage

  1. Run: 
    ./build_installer.sh
    (The script downloads appimagetool automatically if it's missing.)
  2. Output: dist/Silmulator-1.0.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage
  3. Distribute the AppImage; users mark it executable and run it: 
    chmod +x Silmulator-1.0.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage
./Silmulator-1.0.0-linux-x86_64.AppImage

Windows → .exe or .zip

  1. Open Command Prompt (not PowerShell — the script is a .bat).
  2. Optionally install NSIS 3.x for a proper installer .exe.
  3. Run: 
    build_installer.bat
  4. Output (with NSIS): dist\Silmulator-1.0.0-windows-installer.exe
    Output (without NSIS): dist\Silmulator-1.0.0-windows.zip — unzip and run Silmulator.exe inside.

05 Comparison — When to Use Which

Method Python needed? Needs display? Best for
python main.py ✓ Yes ✓ Native display Active development on any OS
uv run python main.py ✓ Yes (uv handles venv) ✓ Native display Dev — fastest first-time setup
silmulator (installed) ✓ Yes ✓ Native display Dev on a configured machine
Docker (browser / NoVNC) ✗ No ✗ No — browser only CI, remote machines, any OS with zero setup
Docker (dev / X11 forward) ✗ No ~ X11 server needed Dev inside container, live code edits
.dmg / .AppImage / .exe ✗ No — self-contained ✓ Native display Distributing to end users with no Python
💡
Often confused: Docker NoVNC mode vs X11 forwarding. NoVNC renders inside a full virtual X11 session inside the container and streams it to the browser — no local X server needed, works on any OS. X11 forwarding (dev mode) sends Qt draw calls to your local X server — faster and feels more native, but requires XQuartz (Mac), VcXsrv (Win), or a running X11 server (Linux).

Check Your Understanding

Q1. You want to run Silmulator on a remote Linux CI server with no display. Which launch method works?

  • python main.py directly on the server
  • docker compose up -d, then access via browser at :6080
  • Run the Linux AppImage on the server
  • uv run python main.py — uv handles the display setup

Q2. After running pip install -e ., which command launches Silmulator?

  • silmulator-gui (the gui-script entry is the only one)
  • silmulator
  • python main.py (the installed entry-point is only for packaged releases)
  • sil (short alias registered in setup.py)

Q3. On macOS, a user double-clicks Silmulator.app from the DMG and gets "Silmulator can't be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software." What is the quickest fix that does NOT require code-signing?

  • Disable Gatekeeper entirely: sudo spctl --master-disable
  • Run chmod +x Silmulator.app in Terminal first
  • Right-click (Control-click) → Open → confirm in the dialog
  • Drag to Applications first, then double-click from there

Q4. The Windows installer build produces a .zip instead of a .exe installer. Why?

  • PyInstaller on Windows always outputs a .zip; NSIS converts it to .exe later in a separate step.
  • Python is below 3.11, so NSIS cannot produce an .exe for that version.
  • NSIS (makensis) is not installed or not on PATH — the .bat falls back to zipping the PyInstaller output.
  • The machine is running Windows 10 or below; the .exe installer requires Windows 11.

Q5. You clone the repo on macOS and run uv sync — what does that do, specifically?

  • Compiles the C++ SCPI extension and installs all Python deps into the system Python.
  • Updates uv.lock to the latest package versions and installs them.
  • Creates (or updates) .venv with the exact package versions from uv.lock, without touching the system Python.
  • Syncs the local package cache with the PyPI remote index — downloads any packages that are out of date.

A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.
Lesson 0001 already covers the basic "how to use" workflow. Before duplicating it, let me check what specifically they haven't seen yet and pick the right next depth level.

"""Code input block — paste C/C++/Python code and extract SCPI calls.

Two input modes are supported:

* **Snippet mode** — double-click the block, paste a single buffer, parse.
* **Project mode** — right-click → "Load project folder" and point at a
  flight OS / RTOS / firmware tree. Every recognized source file is parsed
  and each parsed call can be routed to the connected hardware blocks in
  file/line order, the way a real HIL/SIL test driver would.
"""

from __future__ import annotations
from pathlib import Path
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple

from PyQt6.QtCore import QRectF, Qt
from PyQt6.QtGui import QPainter, QColor, QPen, QBrush, QFont
from PyQt6.QtWidgets import (
    QMenu, QDialog, QVBoxLayout, QHBoxLayout, QTextEdit,
    QPushButton, QLabel, QComboBox, QListWidget, QSplitter, QFileDialog,
    QMessageBox,
)

from silmulator.gui.blocks.base_block import BaseBlock
from silmulator.code_parser import CodeParser, CodeProject, ParsedCommand


class CodeInputBlock(BaseBlock):
    """A block for pasting user code that drives connected hardware blocks.

    Parses C, C++, and Python code to extract SCPI commands,
    then routes those commands to connected hardware blocks.
    """

    BLOCK_WIDTH = 240
    BLOCK_HEIGHT = 160
    HEADER_COLOR = QColor(60, 60, 60)
    BODY_COLOR = QColor(245, 245, 245)

    def __init__(self) -> None:
        from silmulator.devices.base_device import BaseDevice
        super().__init__(_NullDevice(), "Code Input")
        self._source_code: str = ""
        self._language: str = "auto"
        self._parsed_commands: List[ParsedCommand] = []
        self._parser = CodeParser()
        self._project: Optional[CodeProject] = None

    def _setup_ports(self) -> None:
        # Output ports to connect to hardware blocks
        self.add_port("OUT1", "OUT1", 1.0, 0.3)
        self.add_port("OUT2", "OUT2", 1.0, 0.5)
        self.add_port("OUT3", "OUT3", 1.0, 0.7)

    def _paint_content(self, painter: QPainter, rect: QRectF) -> None:
        font = QFont("Consolas", 8)
        painter.setFont(font)
        painter.setPen(QPen(QColor(60, 60, 60)))

        y = self.TITLE_HEIGHT + 16
        if self._project is not None:
            painter.drawText(int(rect.x() + 8), y,
                             f"Project: {self._project.root.name}")
            y += 14
            painter.drawText(int(rect.x() + 8), y,
                             f"Files: {self._project.parsed_file_count()}/"
                             f"{self._project.file_count()}")
        else:
            painter.drawText(int(rect.x() + 8), y, f"Language: {self._language}")
            y += 14
            painter.drawText(int(rect.x() + 8), y,
                             f"Code: {len(self._source_code)} chars")
        y += 14
        painter.drawText(int(rect.x() + 8), y,
                         f"SCPI calls found: {len(self._parsed_commands)}")

        if self._parsed_commands:
            y += 14
            painter.setPen(QPen(QColor(80, 80, 200)))
            painter.drawText(int(rect.x() + 8), y, "Recent commands:")
            for cmd in self._parsed_commands[-4:]:
                y += 12
                painter.drawText(int(rect.x() + 14), y,
                                 f"• {cmd.scpi_command[:28]}")

        # Hint
        if not self._source_code and self._project is None:
            painter.setPen(QPen(QColor(160, 160, 160)))
            painter.drawText(int(rect.x() + 8), int(rect.height() - 12),
                             "Double-click to edit, right-click to load folder")

    def mouseDoubleClickEvent(self, event) -> None:
        self._open_editor()

    def _add_device_menu_actions(self, menu: QMenu) -> None:
        menu.addAction("Open code editor", self._open_editor)
        menu.addAction("Load project folder…", self._load_project)
        menu.addAction("Refresh project", self._refresh_project)
        menu.addAction("Run parsed commands", self._run_commands)
        menu.addAction("Clear code", self._clear_code)

class _CodeEditorDialog(QDialog):
    """Multi-pane code editor with live SCPI extraction preview."""

    def __init__(self, code: str, language: str, block: CodeInputBlock) -> None:
        super().__init__()
        self.block = block
        self.setWindowTitle("Code Input Editor")
        self.resize(900, 600)
        self._setup_ui(code, language)

    def _setup_ui(self, code: str, language: str) -> None:
        layout = QVBoxLayout(self)

        # Top bar
        top_bar = QHBoxLayout()
        top_bar.addWidget(QLabel("Language:"))
        self._lang_combo = QComboBox()
        self._lang_combo.addItems(["auto", "c", "cpp", "python"])
        idx = self._lang_combo.findText(language)
        if idx >= 0:
            self._lang_combo.setCurrentIndex(idx)
        top_bar.addWidget(self._lang_combo)
        top_bar.addStretch()
        parse_btn = QPushButton("Parse")
        parse_btn.clicked.connect(self._do_parse)
        top_bar.addWidget(parse_btn)
        layout.addLayout(top_bar)

        # Splitter: code on left, extracted commands on right
        splitter = QSplitter(Qt.Orientation.Horizontal)

        # Code editor
        self._editor = QTextEdit()
        self._editor.setFont(QFont("Consolas", 10))
        self._editor.setPlaceholderText(
            "Paste your C, C++, or Python code here.\n\n"
            "Example (C):\n"
            '  visa_write(dev, "VOLT 5.0");\n'
            '  visa_write(dev, "OUTP ON");\n'
            '  resp = visa_query(dev, "MEAS:VOLT:DC?");'
        )
        self._editor.setPlainText(code)
        splitter.addWidget(self._editor)

        # Extracted commands panel
        right_pane = QVBoxLayout()
        right_widget = QDialog()
        right_layout = QVBoxLayout(right_widget)
        right_layout.addWidget(QLabel("Extracted SCPI Commands:"))
        self._cmd_list = QListWidget()
        self._cmd_list.setFont(QFont("Consolas", 9))
        right_layout.addWidget(self._cmd_list)
        splitter.addWidget(right_widget)
        splitter.setSizes([550, 350])

        layout.addWidget(splitter)

        # Buttons
        btn_layout = QHBoxLayout()
        ok_btn = QPushButton("OK")
        ok_btn.clicked.connect(self.accept)
        cancel_btn = QPushButton("Cancel")
        cancel_btn.clicked.connect(self.reject)
        btn_layout.addStretch()
        btn_layout.addWidget(ok_btn)
        btn_layout.addWidget(cancel_btn)
        layout.addLayout(btn_layout)

        # Initial parse
        self._do_parse()

    def _do_parse(self) -> None:
        from silmulator.code_parser import CodeParser
        parser = CodeParser()
        code = self._editor.toPlainText()
        lang = self._lang_combo.currentText()
        cmds = parser.parse(code, lang)
        self._cmd_list.clear()
        for cmd in cmds:
            self._cmd_list.addItem(
                f"[line {cmd.line_number}] {cmd.scpi_command}"
            )

    def get_code(self) -> str:
        return self._editor.toPlainText()

    def get_language(self) -> str:
        return self._lang_combo.currentText()

        top_bar = QHBoxLayout()
        top_bar.addWidget(QLabel("Language:"))
        self._lang_combo = QComboBox()
        self._lang_combo.addItems(["auto", "c", "cpp", "python"])
        idx = self._lang_combo.findText(language)
        if idx >= 0:
            self._lang_combo.setCurrentIndex(idx)
        top_bar.addWidget(self._lang_combo)
        top_bar.addStretch()
        parse_btn = QPushButton("Parse")
        parse_btn.clicked.connect(self._do_parse)
        top_bar.addWidget(parse_btn)
        layout.addLayout(top_bar)

        # Splitter: code on left, extracted commands on right
        splitter = QSplitter(Qt.Orientation.Horizontal)

        # Code editor
        self._editor = QTextEdit()
        self._editor.setFont(QFont("Consolas", 10))
        self._editor.setPlaceholderText(
            "Paste your C, C++, or Python code here.\n\n"
            "Example (C):\n"
            '  visa_write(dev, "VOLT 5.0");\n'
            '  visa_write(dev, "OUTP ON");\n'
            '  resp = visa_query(dev, "MEAS:VOLT:DC?");'
        )
        self._editor.setPlainText(code)
        splitter.addWidget(self._editor)

        # Extracted commands panel
        right_pane = QVBoxLayout()
        right_widget = QDialog()
        right_layout = QVBoxLayout(right_widget)
        right_layout.addWidget(QLabel("Extracted SCPI Commands:"))
        self._cmd_list = QListWidget()
        self._cmd_list.setFont(QFont("Consolas", 9))
        right_layout.addWidget(self._cmd_list)
        splitter.addWidget(right_widget)
        splitter.setSizes([550, 350])

        layout.addWidget(splitter)

        # Buttons
        btn_layout = QHBoxLayout()
        ok_btn = QPushButton("OK")
        ok_btn.clicked.connect(self.accept)
        cancel_btn = QPushButton("Cancel")
        cancel_btn.clicked.connect(self.reject)
        btn_layout.addStretch()
        btn_layout.addWidget(ok_btn)
        btn_layout.addWidget(cancel_btn)
        layout.addLayout(btn_layout)

        # Initial parse
        self._do_parse()

    def _do_parse(self) -> None:
        from silmulator.code_parser import CodeParser
        parser = CodeParser()
        code = self._editor.toPlainText()
        lang = self._lang_combo.currentText()
        cmds = parser.parse(code, lang)
        self._cmd_list.clear()
        for cmd in cmds:
            self._cmd_list.addItem(
                f"[line {cmd.line_number}] {cmd.scpi_command}"
            )

    def get_code(self) -> str:
        return self._editor.toPlainText()

    def get_language(self) -> str:
        return self._lang_combo.currentText()

Lesson 0004

Running a Complete SIL Test

Paste real firmware code into the Code Input block, wire it to simulated instruments, and watch the SCPI commands flow — this is Silmulator doing its actual job.

Builds on: 0001 (workflow) → 0002 (connections) → 0003 (running the app)

Lesson progress

0 / 6 sections complete

01 The End-to-End Picture

Lesson 0001 showed you the three-step workflow in the abstract: Place → Connect → Drive. This lesson makes it concrete by walking through a real SIL test from start to finish — raw C firmware code in, SCPI responses out.

Here is what happens inside Silmulator from the moment you paste firmware code to the moment the simulated instrument answers:

C / C++ / Python
firmware sourceyour test input
→
CodeParsercode_parser/base_parser.py
→
CodeInputBlock._run_commands()routes to connected blocks
→
Device.process(cmd)simulated instrument responds

Each stage is a real class in the codebase. Understanding this pipeline is the key to knowing what Silmulator can and can't do.

02 Step 1 — Place and Connect the Blocks

For a typical SIL test you need at least two blocks on the canvas:

  • Code Input — the block that holds your firmware source and routes extracted SCPI calls.
  • One or more instrument blocks — the simulated hardware your firmware talks to (Oscilloscope, Power Supply, etc.).
  1. From the Library panel (or Add menu), add a Code Input block and an Oscilloscope block.
  2. Draw a wire from Code Input → OUT1 to Oscilloscope → CH1_IN. The Code Input block has three output ports (OUT1, OUT2, OUT3) on its right edge, one per connected instrument.
  3. If your code talks to multiple instruments (e.g. a power supply and an oscilloscope), add each instrument, wire a separate OUT port to each one.
ℹ️
The Code Input block's three OUT ports are defined in silmulator/gui/blocks/code_input_block.py:51-53: 
add_port("OUT1", "OUT1", 1.0, 0.3)   # right edge, 30% down
add_port("OUT2", "OUT2", 1.0, 0.5)   # right edge, 50% down
add_port("OUT3", "OUT3", 1.0, 0.7)   # right edge, 70% down
x_frac=1.0 puts them on the right edge; y_frac positions them vertically.

03 Step 2 — Paste and Parse Your Firmware Code

Double-click the Code Input block to open the code editor. Paste your C, C++, or Python code on the left; the right pane shows extracted SCPI commands in real time when you click Parse.

What the parser recognises

The parser (silmulator/code_parser/base_parser.py) scans each line against a list of known C/C++ and Python patterns. These are the C patterns it looks for:

# C/C++ write patterns (from C_WRITE_PATTERNS in base_parser.py)
viWrite(session, "VOLT 5.0")         ✓ extracted
visa_write(dev, "OUTP ON")            ✓ extracted
scpi_send(handle, "ACQ:STATE 1")       ✓ extracted
ibwrt(dev, "TRIG:A:LEVEL 1.5")       ✓ extracted

# C/C++ query patterns
result = viQueryF(session, "MEAS:VOLT:DC?")  ✓ extracted as query

# Python patterns
inst.write("VOLT 5.0")                ✓ extracted
result = inst.query("MEAS:VOLT:DC?")   ✓ extracted as query

After extraction each command becomes a ParsedCommand object:

silmulator/code_parser/base_parser.py
@dataclass
class ParsedCommand:
    scpi_command: str        # e.g. "VOLT 5.0" or "MEAS:VOLT:DC?"
    line_number:  int        # where it appeared in the source
    source_language: str    # "c" or "python"
    context:  str = ""      # first 80 chars of the original line
    is_query: bool = False  # True if ends with ?
    variable_name: Optional[str] = None  # e.g. "result" for query assignments

The block face shows a live tally: "SCPI calls found: 6" and a preview of the last four commands.

⚠️
The SCPI heuristic is not infallible. The parser uses a regex that matches strings starting with *WORD or WORD[:] — it can miss commands buried in preprocessor macros, variadic format strings, or indirect string construction. Real embedded code that builds SCPI strings dynamically (e.g. sprintf(buf, "VOLT %f", v)) will be extracted as VOLT <VAR> — the variable part is replaced with the literal <VAR> placeholder.

04 Step 3 — Run and Read the Responses

Right-click the Code Input block → Run parsed commands. This calls _run_commands():

silmulator/gui/blocks/code_input_block.py:163
def _run_commands(self) -> None:
    """Route parsed SCPI commands to connected blocks."""
    if not self._parsed_commands:
        return
    connected_blocks = self._get_connected_blocks()
    for parsed_cmd in self._parsed_commands:
        for block in connected_blocks:
            block.send_command(parsed_cmd.scpi_command)

Key things to notice:

  • _get_connected_blocks() walks all three OUT ports and collects every instrument on the other end of a wire. If you have two instruments wired up, every parsed command is sent to both — there is no routing-by-instrument-type. Connect only the instruments your firmware actually talks to.
  • block.send_command() calls the instrument's device.process(cmd) which returns the SCPI response. Responses appear in the block's SCPI Console panel (bottom of the window) or in the block's right-click context menu output.

What does the instrument actually do with the command string? It goes through the ScpiParser:

silmulator/scpi/parser.py
@dataclass
class ScpiCommand:
    path:     str         # e.g. "MEAS:VOLT:DC" (normalised, no ?)
    is_query: bool        # True if ends with ?
    params:   List[str]   # e.g. ["5.0"] for "VOLT 5.0"

The parser splits compound commands on ;, strips the ? suffix, uppercases the header path, and separates parameters. The device handler then looks up the path in its command table and either sets a value or returns one.

Interpreting responses

Command typeWhat it doesResponse
VOLT 5.0Sets power supply channel voltage(empty — write-only)
OUTP ONEnables output(empty)
MEAS:VOLT:DC?Query: read measured voltage5.00001 (set value + noise)
ACQ:STATE 1Starts acquisition on oscilloscope(empty)
CURVE?Transfers waveform dataASCII comma-separated floats
*IDN?Instrument identificationSilmulator,Oscilloscope,...

05 Snippet Mode vs Project Mode

The Code Input block has two input modes. Both end up in the same parse → run pipeline; the difference is how you get code in.

ModeHow to activateWhat it parsesBest for
Snippet Double-click the block A single text buffer you paste manually Quick experiments, one-off command sequences
Project Right-click → "Load project folder…" Every .c, .cpp, .py file in the chosen directory tree, in file/line order Full firmware trees (RTOS, flight SW), full-system SIL runs

In project mode the block face shows:

Project: my_firmware/
Files: 12/47  ← parsed / total recognised
SCPI calls found: 38

The "Right-click → Refresh project" action re-parses all files without closing the block — useful when you edit the firmware and want to re-run immediately.

💡
Often confused: "Run parsed commands" vs "Send SCPI command" (in the SCPI Console). Run parsed commands fires the entire list extracted from source code, in order, broadcasting to all connected instruments. Send SCPI command sends a single command you type manually to the selected block. Use the Console for interactive debugging; use Run for automated replay of your firmware's command sequence.

Check Your Understanding

Q1. You paste firmware C code into snippet mode and click Parse. The right panel shows zero commands. Your code contains scpi_send(handle, "ACQ:STATE 1");. What is the most likely cause?

  • scpi_send is not a recognised C pattern — only viWrite and ibwrt are supported.
  • The language dropdown is set to 'auto' and auto-detection picked 'python' instead of 'c', skipping all C_WRITE_PATTERNS.
  • The Code Input block is not connected to any instrument block yet, so Parse returns nothing.
  • The _deduplicate() method removed the command because it appears twice in the code.

Q2. _run_commands() loops over connected_blocks for every parsed command. Your Code Input has OUT1 wired to a Power Supply and OUT2 wired to an Oscilloscope. What happens when the firmware contains both VOLT 5.0 and ACQ:STATE 1?

  • VOLT 5.0 goes only to the Power Supply; ACQ:STATE 1 goes only to the Oscilloscope — Silmulator routes by command prefix.
  • Both VOLT 5.0 and ACQ:STATE 1 are sent to both the Power Supply and the Oscilloscope; each instrument silently ignores commands it doesn't recognise.
  • Only the first parsed command is sent; run must be clicked once per command to advance through the list.
  • The run raises an error because VOLT is not a valid oscilloscope command.

Q3. Your C firmware uses sprintf(buf, "VOLT %f", voltage); visa_write(dev, buf); to build a command dynamically. What does the Code Input block extract?

  • It extracts the correct command with the runtime value of voltage substituted in.
  • It extracts the sprintf format string literally — something like VOLT %f — because the parser reads string literals, not runtime variable values.
  • It extracts nothing — the parser skips sprintf() because it's a formatting call, not a VISA call.
  • It extracts the command once for each unique value of voltage it can infer from the source code.

Q4. In project mode you load a firmware folder. The block face shows "Files: 12/47". What does the 47 represent?

  • The total number of instrument blocks Silmulator supports connecting at once.
  • The total number of SCPI commands found across all files (12 matched, 47 total).
  • The total number of source files found in the folder tree; 12 of them were successfully parsed.
  • The number of files still pending — 12 are loaded; 47 remain to be loaded on the next refresh.

Q5. You run parsed commands against the Power Supply. The SCPI Console shows a response of 5.00001 for MEAS:VOLT:DC? even though you set VOLT 5.0. Is this a bug?

  • Yes — the power supply block is miscalibrated and needs reset with *RST before measurements are reliable.
  • No — Silmulator intentionally adds small Gaussian noise (~1e-5 relative) to measurements to mimic real instrument behavior.
  • Yes — you need to issue *RST after setting VOLT to flush the noise accumulator.
  • Yes — the C++ SCPI parser is not built, so the Python fallback introduces extra floating-point rounding.

# Fix hardware block connections not working / not visible in the GUI

## Context

User report: wires between hardware blocks don't get created, the "first entry point"
(first-added block's ports) is not connecting, and ports/wires are not showing in the GUI.
Symptoms confirmed: failure during drag, on release, after save/reopen, and ports not visible —
across all block types.

Diagnosis (all root causes identified by reading the code; the existing
`tests/test_canvas_connections.py` suite bypasses the real Qt mouse path, which is why it
passes while the GUI misbehaves):

1. **Rubber-band hijacks the wire drag.** `CanvasScene.mousePressEvent` /
   `mouseReleaseEvent` (Silmulator/silmulator/gui/canvas.py:167-194) handle the port click
   but never call `event.accept()`. `QGraphicsView` is in `RubberBandDrag` mode
   (canvas.py:304); an unaccepted left-press makes the view start a rubber-band selection
   that draws over the drag, churns the scene selection on every move, and fights the
   dashed temp wire → "no wire shows while dragging".

2. **New blocks stack on top of each other, burying the first block's ports.**
   - Toolbar buttons add every block at fixed `QPointF(200, 150)` (main_window.py:246).
   - Add-menu adds every block at fixed `QPointF(100, 100)` (main_window.py:215).
   - Library panel spaces blocks `260`px apart (main_window.py:72-75) but blocks are up to
     300px wide (OscilloscopeBlock) / 280 (MSP430) → guaranteed overlap.
   Newer blocks render above older ones, so the first block's edge ports become invisible /
   unclickable, and wires (z = -1, intentionally below blocks) are hidden under the overlap
   → "first entry point not connecting / not showing".

3. **Save → reopen silently drops Function Generator blocks and all their wires.**
   `FunctionGeneratorBlock.__init__` passes device_type `"Function Gen"`
   (function_generator_block.py:35) but the registry key is `"Function Generator"`
   (canvas.py:31). `to_dict` stores `device_type`; `from_dict` → `add_block("Function Gen")`
   → `BLOCK_REGISTRY.get(...)` → `None` → block skipped, and every wire referencing it is
   dropped (canvas.py:279-294).

4. **File → New leaves dangling block/wire references.** `MainWindow._new_canvas`
   (main_window.py:277) calls `QGraphicsScene.clear()`, which deletes the C++ items but
   leaves `CanvasScene._blocks` / `_wires` populated → stale counts, and the next save /
   reset-all touches deleted items (RuntimeError). Related to the save/reopen symptom.

## Changes

### 1. `Silmulator/silmulator/gui/canvas.py`
- `mousePressEvent`: when a port is found, call `event.accept()` before returning.
- `mouseReleaseEvent`: when finishing a wire drag, call `event.accept()` before returning.
- `mouseMoveEvent`: while `self._connecting`, call `event.accept()` before the early return.
- Override `clear()` on `CanvasScene` to call `super().clear()` and reset `_blocks`,
  `_wires`, `_connecting`, `_temp_wire` (and have `from_dict` use it instead of its own
  partial reset).
- Add `CanvasScene.find_free_position(block_cls) -> QPointF`: scan grid slots
  (left-to-right, top-to-bottom, snapped to `GRID_SIZE`) and return the first position
  where the candidate rect (block width/height + a margin for edge ports, ~20px) does not
  intersect any existing block's scene rect. Allow `add_block(device_type, pos=None)` to
  use it when no position is given.

### 2. `Silmulator/silmulator/gui/main_window.py`
- `BlockLibraryPanel._add_block`, toolbar button handler, and Add-menu handler: stop
  passing fixed/overlapping positions — call `canvas.add_block(name)` and let
  `find_free_position` place the block.
- `_new_canvas`: rely on the fixed `CanvasScene.clear()` (no other change needed).

### 3. `Silmulator/silmulator/gui/blocks/function_generator_block.py`
- `super().__init__(FunctionGenerator(), "Function Generator")` — must equal the
  `BLOCK_REGISTRY` key so save/load round-trips.

## Tests (`Silmulator/tests/`)

- `test_canvas_connections.py` additions:
  - **End-to-end mouse test through the real Qt path** using `PyQt6.QtTest.QTest` on a
    `CanvasView` viewport (offscreen platform already forced in conftest): add two blocks,
    press on src port, move, release on dst port; assert a `WireItem` exists and no
    rubber-band selection replaced it. This is the regression test for the missing
    `event.accept()` — it fails the current code via the rubber-band path where the
    synthetic-call tests pass.
- `test_block_creation.py` additions:
  - Parametrized over `BLOCK_REGISTRY`: `block.device_type` must be a key of
    `BLOCK_REGISTRY` (catches the "Function Gen" mismatch for every current/future block).
  - Auto-placement: adding N blocks with no position produces pairwise non-intersecting
    scene rects.
  - `clear()` resets state: after `scene.clear()`, `scene.blocks == []` and
    `to_dict() == {"blocks": [], "wires": []}`.
- New round-trip test: build a scene with one of each block type + wires, `to_dict` →
  fresh scene `from_dict` → assert same block types and same wire count (catches #3).

## Verification

1. `cd Silmulator && QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen python -m pytest tests/ -q` — full suite
   (288 existing tests) plus new tests green. (Resolve the python/uv toolchain first —
   `python` was not on PATH; use the project `.venv` or `uv run`.)
2. Confirm the new QTest end-to-end test fails on the unfixed code (run it before applying
   the canvas.py fix) — proves it covers the real bug.
3. Offscreen smoke script: construct `MainWindow`, add three blocks via the same handlers
   the toolbar uses, assert non-overlapping positions, save to dict, reload, assert all
   blocks/wires present.
4. Per CLAUDE.md: run the `reviewer` subagent before committing; commit as
   `fix(gui): ...` on the `fix_hardware_connectors` branch.

## Out of scope (noted for later, per "don't fix unrelated")
- GNU-Radio-style click-then-click connecting (current model is press-drag-release only).
- Input/output port direction enforcement (already in the project TODO list).

skills.name: teach
skills.content:
The user wants to learn "do" (or, if blank, you choose the most valuable concept to teach next based on their progress and this project's code). This is a STATEFUL, multi-session teaching relationship. Treat the folder `docs/learning/` as the teaching workspace. Learning persists there between sessions. Read what already exists before teaching anything new. ## The Core Difference From Generic Teaching Everything you teach must be grounded in THIS project. You are not teaching abstract computer science — you are teaching the concepts that show up in the code the user is actually writing, using their own files as examples. Abstract knowledge that isn't tied to their project will not stick. ## Workspace Files (read these first if they exist) - `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md` — what the user has learned so far, what they found hard, what to teach next. Your map of their knowledge. If it doesn't exist, create it on the first lesson. - `docs/learning/GLOSSARY.md` — terms the user now understands. Only add a term here once they've demonstrably grasped it. All lessons should use terminology consistent with this glossary. - `docs/learning/lessons/*.html` — the lessons themselves, numbered `0001-.html` and incrementing. These are the main artifact. ## Step 1 — Ground the Lesson Before teaching, establish two things: **Relevance to the project:** Where does this concept appear in the codebase? Grep/read to find the actual files, classes, or functions that use it. If the concept isn't in the project yet but is about to be (the user is heading there), say so. If it has nothing to do with the project, gently check whether they want a project-grounded lesson or just a general explanation. **The right difficulty (zone of proximal development):** Read PROGRESS.md. Teach the thing that builds on what they know and is challenging but not overwhelming. Keep scope tight — one concept taught well beats five rushed. If they say they already know something, record that in PROGRESS.md and move to the next useful thing. ## Step 2 — Gather Trustworthy Knowledge Do not rely only on your own parametric knowledge for technical specifics — it can be outdated or subtly wrong. For anything where accuracy matters (library behavior, protocol specs, version-specific details), web-search to ground the explanation in current, authoritative sources. Note the sources. ## Step 3 — Produce an HTML Lesson Create a self-contained, single-file HTML lesson saved to `docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-.html` (increment NNNN from the highest existing lesson; start at 0001). The HTML must be: **Self-contained** — all CSS and JS inline, no external dependencies, opens correctly with a plain `file://` open in any browser. **Beautiful and readable** — clean typography, comfortable line length, good contrast, syntax-highlighted code blocks (a small inline highlighter or hand-applied span colors are fine), responsive. This should feel like a polished lesson, not a wall of text. **Structured** with these sections: 1. Title and a one-line "why this matters for [project]" 2. The concept explained plainly (the knowledge) 3. A minimal standalone example, heavily commented 4. "In this project" — the real code from their repo that uses this, with the actual file path shown, walked through line by line 5. "Often confused with" — when a similar concept exists, contrast them clearly (what they share, where they diverge, when to use each). Examples of pairs worth contrasting: container vs VM, process vs thread, concurrency vs parallelism, class vs instance, argument vs parameter, sync vs async, compiler vs interpreter, declaration vs definition. 6. Interactive practice (the skill): 3-5 quiz questions or small in-browser exercises with immediate feedback. Use inline JS so clicking an answer instantly shows whether it's right and why. This tight feedback loop is where skill actually forms — don't skip it. CRITICAL — randomize answer position. A common failure is putting the correct answer first every time, which trains the user to click the top option instead of thinking. Prevent this STRUCTURALLY, not by hoping: - Do NOT encode correctness by position (never "the answer is option A" or "index 0 is correct"). - Mark the correct option with a data attribute, e.g. `data-correct="true"`, and give wrong options `data-correct="false"`. - Have the JavaScript SHUFFLE the options in the DOM on page load (e.g. a Fisher-Yates shuffle of each question's option elements), so the rendered order is randomized every time the page opens. - The click handler checks the clicked element's `data-correct` attribute, never its position. This makes "always first" impossible regardless of the order you authored them in. - Also vary the authored order yourself as a backstop — don't write every correct answer first in the source either. - Each option should carry its own short explanation (why it's right or wrong) shown on click, so distractors teach too. 7. A short "check your understanding" set of scenario questions. **Progress-aware** — include a simple completion mechanism: checkboxes or a "mark complete" button for each section, with state held in-page via JS (plain variables/DOM state, NOT localStorage — that's unreliable here). At minimum, the quiz should show a score. The goal is the user can see how far they've gotten through the lesson. ### Reference pattern for shuffled quiz options Follow this structure so the correct answer is never tied to position: ```html

Which SCPI command queries DC voltage?

  • MEAS:VOLT:DC?
  • SET:VOLT:DC
  • VOLT:DC 3.3

``` The key line is `li.dataset.correct === 'true'` — correctness comes from the attribute, and `shuffle` reorders the DOM on load, so position is meaningless. ## Step 4 — Make It Trivial to Open After writing the file, give the user the exact command to open it: - macOS: `open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` - Linux: `xdg-open docs/learning/lessons/NNNN-name.html` Print the right one for their platform. ## Step 5 — Discuss and Refine Invite questions. Answer them directly. If a question reveals the explainer was unclear, amend the HTML or add a follow-up lesson. Once it's clear the user understands a term, add it to GLOSSARY.md using a concise definition. ## Step 6 — Record Progress Update `docs/learning/PROGRESS.md`: - What was taught this session (link the lesson file) - How well the user seemed to grasp it - What they struggled with - A suggested next concept, tied to the project and their current level ## Step 7 — Knowledge Check Before Closing End the session with 2-3 spoken (in-chat) questions that verify the lesson landed. Let the user attempt them; correct gently with reference back to the lesson. This is the retention check that flat documents skip. ## Tone Encouraging but honest. The user is building real skills they'll rely on to maintain this codebase alone. Challenge them appropriately. Never pad. The HTML lesson is the durable artifact; the chat is the live tutoring around it.
